text: Silo is rebuilt piece by piece, carefully, one feature the owner took at a time, in the order of the list. The list is sorted so that the most certain and most useful features come first and every cut from the top is a product.
One main computer, the user's agent lives inside it, and forks and disposable computers serve tasks. An agent on the user's Mac driving Silo is not the main path.
Agents inside a computer get every tool, scoped by where they are: anything the user could do in the app. A computer cannot get more than it has, and anything that widens access asks the user.

"Git for computers" is the framing, and the words are Git's: one verb, merge (fast-forward when main is unchanged, item by item with conflicts asked otherwise), plus replace main. Fold, keep and promote are not used.
The engine is written in Zig. It is the core piece: performant, secure, easy to reason about. The app, the command line and every tool only talk to it. Its design is data first, with events.
The Mac app is written in Swift, comes first, and holds no logic. macOS computers are driven from Swift directly, never through Rust bindings.
The engine also runs on Linux, to use a Linux machine as a host.
Properties are stated and checked as we build: state properties, formal verification, whatever shows what always holds.

The old code stays outside this tree. It is read only when needed, through a fresh agent dedicated to that lookup, which brings back only what is relevant. Parts may be moved across, reviewed and cleaned up.
The first user is the owner, on a Mac. A developer in a company fits the same product. Team features come later, on the same product.

The agent is considered hostile. Rules exist to make an attack predictable: a hostile agent can do what the rules allow and nothing else. No destination is special: the user sets the rules for GitHub like for everything else. Silo is as secure as the rules the user sets, and it makes a secure setup as easy as the rest.
Security is built properly and is not the current focus.
macOS and Linux computers are consistent: the same page in the app, the same image contents, an image upgrade path.
A task started from outside starts from a recipe or a checkpoint, so it has no setup to wait for. Updating main after a pull request merges is an ordinary pull, not a Silo feature.
GitHub is the Workshop's storage: issues of this repository, no database of ours and no separate backups. Agents post as a bot, not under the owner's name.

The Workshop is a public page of silo.amontlabs.com that shows the plan as a map of the product's parts. The owner decides there; anyone signed in with GitHub can comment, vote and suggest features. Visitors see the plan; the decisions are shown to the owner only.
What Silo is belongs on the home page, not in the Workshop.
Recordings are committed to the repository as files and played on the site.
Pages for people must be obvious to use and short on text: one place to look, no explanatory paragraphs, no assistant-sounding copy.
A doc that no longer describes the code is deleted, not moved to an archive.
No time estimates and no plans built from dates.
Agents may push to this repository's remote. The old history stays on the branch `legacy`.
